analysis.investment_thesis: A five-year-old ferrous castings micro-cap with gaudy reported ROE (51%) but chronically negative free cash flow (-1, -9, -7, -3 Cr across four years) — the accounting returns aren't turning into owner earnings. Invert: recently IPO'd (equity jumped 20→123 Cr in FY25), commodity industry, no track record through a cycle — this is speculation dressed up as quality.
key_strengths: Headline ROCE 46% and ROE 51% with rapid revenue scaling (5→71 Cr, 142% CAGR)
Operating margins expanded materially (OI 0→23 Cr) and debt kept modest (14 Cr vs 123 Cr equity post-IPO)
Promoter holding high at 70%, so incentives at least nominally aligned
key_risks: FCF negative every year (cum. ~-20 Cr) despite reported PAT — earnings quality is poor; growth funded by IPO + debt
Incorporated Jan 2020 — no cycle-tested track record in a cyclical castings/forgings industry with little pricing power
Tiny scale (71 Cr revenue, 302 Cr mcap) on BSE with thin float — volatile, illiquid, easy to manipulate
red_flags: Persistent OCF < Net Profit and zero cumulative FCF while PAT compounds — classic working-capital/capex-funded earnings
Equity base ballooned 6x in one year (fresh issue) — returns on new capital unproven
Customized ferrous castings is a low-moat, customer-concentrated business; 51% ROE at this maturity is suspicious
analysis.detailed_analysis: Invert first: what makes this a bad investment? A company five years old, in a capital-intensive, cyclical, commodity-adjacent business (ferrous castings), with FCF of -1, -9, -7, -3 Cr over four consecutive years, yet reporting 46% ROCE. The reported profitability and the cash register are telling different stories — Investing CF of -17 Cr in FY25 vs OCF of 12 Cr means every rupee of operating cash (and then some) is being consumed by capex/working capital. Reserves leapt from 16 to 104 Cr in FY25 not from retained earnings but from a share issuance. Buying this is buying a prospectus, not a proven compounder.\n\nOn valuation, 20x earnings for a micro-cap with one good year of scale and no FCF is not cheap — it is a bet that today's margins and growth persist against competitors who can buy the same induction furnaces. I have no way to assess management's intellectual honesty or capital allocation discipline with this short a history. Munger's rule applies: when in doubt, do nothing. This goes in the "too hard / too new" pile. Pass, watch it survive a down-cycle, then revisit in 2030.
